questions.prompt: In the V-model diagram, which testing level is paired with Requirement Gathering on the opposite side of the V?
options: Acceptance Testing
System Testing
Integration Testing
Unit Testing
Static Testing
questions.explanation: In the V-model, Requirement Gathering is paired with Acceptance Testing; System Analysis pairs with System Testing, Software Design with Integration Testing and Module Design with Unit Testing.

questions.prompt: Which question summarizes verification?
options: Are we building the product right?
Are we building the right product?
Does the test look at the code?
Does the test execute the code?
Is the test based on spec or on use?
questions.explanation: Verification asks 'Are we building the product right?' and checks conformance to specs; 'Are we building the right product?' is validation, which checks fitness for purpose with stakeholders.

questions.prompt: In the V-lifecycle testing diagram, which pairing of testing approach and lifecycle levels is shown?
options: Black-box — Specification and SW Integration
White-box — Analysis and System Test
Random test — Design and Unit Test
White-box — Specification and SW Integration
White-box — Analysis and Specification
questions.explanation: The V-lifecycle diagram groups Specification and SW Integration as black-box, Design, Implementation and Unit Test as white-box, and Analysis and System Test as random test.

questions.prompt: What characterizes black-box testing?
options: The internal structure and code are hidden; nothing is known about them
The tester knows the internal structure and code of the software
The code is evaluated without the program being executed
Test inputs are chosen at random instead of from a specification
Each individual unit is tested in isolation by its developer
questions.explanation: In black-box testing the internal structure, program or code is hidden and nothing is known about it; knowing the internal structure is white-box testing.

questions.prompt: A tester reads a method's source code, designs inputs to reach each branch, and then runs those tests. How is this testing classified?
options: Dynamic and white-box
Static and white-box
Dynamic and black-box
Static and black-box
Random and black-box
questions.explanation: Running the tests executes the code, so it is dynamic, and designing them from the source code means the tester looks at the code, so it is white-box.

questions.prompt: What problem are unit testing frameworks such as JUnit and NUnit meant to address?
options: Testing is not closely integrated with development, so progress cannot be measured
Production code cannot be compiled until a full system test has been run
GUI tests cannot be automated, so every user journey must be checked by hand
Requirements cannot be reviewed with stakeholders before coding starts
Developers cannot deploy to production without an independent test team
questions.explanation: JUnit/NUnit address the problem that testing is not closely integrated with development, which prevents measuring progress; their philosophy is to develop tests in parallel with the application code or before it.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches the testing percentages recommended in the course?
options: System tests verify class interactions and make up 20% of tests
Unit tests verify class interactions and make up 20% of tests
GUI tests verify end-to-end journeys and make up 70% of tests
Unit tests verify end-to-end journeys and make up 10% of tests
System tests verify a single class and make up 70% of tests
questions.explanation: The slide gives unit tests (behavior of a single class) 70%, system tests (class interactions) 20% and GUI tests (end-to-end journeys) 10% of all tests.

questions.prompt: In the test pyramid diagram, what changes as you move up from unit tests toward UI and manual tests?
options: More integration and slower tests
More isolation and faster tests
More isolation but slower tests
More integration but faster tests
More tests and a lower cost per test
questions.explanation: The pyramid's arrows point to more integration and slower tests toward the top (UI and manual tests), and to more isolation and faster tests toward unit tests at the base.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches the Units diagram that compares E2E, service and unit scopes?
options: A unit is one Func() or a small group of Func()s in a service
A unit spans the user interface and several microservices
The E2E scope covers only one Func() and its database
The service scope covers the user interface and all microservices
A unit must always include the service's database
questions.explanation: The diagram shows one Unit bracket around a single Func() and another around a small group of Func()s inside the service; the E2E scope is the one that spans the user interface and the microservices.

questions.prompt: In the TestNG CalculatorTest class, what does the @BeforeMethod-annotated setUp() method do?
options: Creates a new Calculator before each test method runs
Creates one Calculator after all test methods finish
Runs as an extra test that must pass before testAdd()
Asserts that the Calculator constructor throws no errors
Resets the test results after each failed assertion
questions.explanation: The @BeforeMethod setUp() runs before each test method and assigns a new Calculator, so every test starts with a fresh object; it is setup code, not a test itself.

questions.prompt: Calculator.add returns a + b and subtract returns a - b. CalculatorTest asserts that add(5, 3) equals 8 and subtract(5, 3) equals 2. What does the TestNG run report?
options: Tests run: 2, Failures: 0, Skips: 0
Tests run: 2, Failures: 1, Skips: 0
Tests run: 2, Failures: 0, Skips: 1
Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Skips: 0
Tests run: 3, Failures: 0, Skips: 0
questions.explanation: Both @Test methods, testAdd and testSubtract, pass because add and subtract are implemented correctly, so TestNG reports 2 tests run with 0 failures and 0 skips; setUp() is not counted as a test.

questions.prompt: What is the role of assertions in a unit test?
options: They express requirements the unit must meet, replacing human checking
They create the objects and input values that the test needs before it runs
They call the method under test with the inputs prepared for the test
They replace slow dependencies so that the unit can run in isolation
They record how long each test method takes to finish executing
questions.explanation: Assertions ensure the code behaves as expected: they express the requirements the unit under test must meet and replace humans in checking that the software does what it should; creating objects is Arrange and calling the method is Act.

questions.prompt: In the C# BankTests project (Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting), which attributes mark the test class and a test method?
options: [TestClass] and [TestMethod]
[TestClass] and [Test]
@BeforeMethod and @Test
[UnitTest] and [TestMethod]
[TestSuite] and [TestCase]
questions.explanation: The BankAccountTests class is marked [TestClass] and its test methods [TestMethod]; @BeforeMethod and @Test are the TestNG annotations from the Java example.

questions.prompt: In the Debit_WithValidAmount_UpdatesBalance test, what happens in the Arrange section?
options: The starting values and the BankAccount under test are set up
account.Debit(debitAmount) is called on the account object
The actual balance is compared with the expected value 7.44
The intentionally incorrect Debit code is corrected first
The class is marked with [TestClass] so that it can run
questions.explanation: Arrange sets beginningBalance, debitAmount and expected and creates the BankAccount; calling Debit is the Act step and comparing actual with expected is the Assert step.

questions.prompt: The BankAccount.Debit method contains intentionally incorrect code. Which change fixes it so that the debit test passes?
options: Replace m_balance += amount with m_balance -= amount
Replace amount > m_balance with amount < m_balance
Remove the check that throws when amount < 0
Replace m_balance -= amount with m_balance += amount
Make m_balance a readonly field like m_customerName
questions.explanation: Debit wrongly adds the amount to the balance (m_balance += amount, marked as intentionally incorrect); the fix replaces it with m_balance -= amount, after which the test passes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is listed as a benefit of unit testing?
options: Facilitation of refactoring
No ongoing maintenance of test cases
Thorough testing of user interfaces
Independence from the developers
Full coverage of interactions between units
questions.explanation: Facilitation of refactoring is one of the seven listed benefits; maintenance overhead, dependence on developers, and difficulty testing user interfaces and interactions are listed as disadvantages.

questions.prompt: Why is over-reliance on automated unit tests listed as a disadvantage?
options: It can create a false sense of security about remaining bugs
Automated unit tests cannot run inside a CI/CD pipeline
Automated unit tests always run slower than manual tests
Automation makes ongoing test maintenance unnecessary
Automated unit tests can only check the user interface
questions.explanation: Over-reliance on automation can lead to a false sense of security, because automated tests may not uncover all possible issues or bugs.

questions.prompt: A project relies only on unit tests, and later bugs appear in how two modules exchange data. Which disadvantage of unit testing does this illustrate?
options: Difficulty in testing interactions
Difficulty in testing user interfaces
Maintenance overhead
Dependence on developers
Time and effort
questions.explanation: Unit testing focuses only on individual units, so it may not be sufficient for testing interactions between units.

questions.prompt: A developer writes the unit tests for a new feature before writing the feature's code. Which practice is this?
options: Test-Driven Development (TDD)
Manual unit testing
Continuous delivery
Black-box system testing
Static testing
questions.explanation: In Test-Driven Development, developers write tests before writing the actual code; manual unit testing means checking each part by hand without special tools.

questions.prompt: In the example CI/CD setup, a Git user pushes code to a GitHub repository that contains unit tests. What happens next?
options: A Git webhook triggers AWS CodeBuild, so the unit tests run automatically
A tester manually runs the unit tests before the next release date
The unit tests run only after the code is deployed to production
AWS CodeBuild sends the code back to the user for a manual review
The repository waits for the weekly scheduled test run to start
questions.explanation: The push to the repository fires a Git webhook to AWS CodeBuild; in CI/CD, unit tests run automatically whenever new code is added instead of being run by hand.

questions.prompt: Why is manual unit testing not used much, according to the course?
options: It costs more and must be repeated every time the code changes
It requires special testing tools that developers do not have
Developers are not allowed to test their own code by hand
It can only be applied to graphical user interfaces
It can only start after the system has been deployed
questions.explanation: Manual unit testing costs more because people are paid for their testing time and takes a lot of time because tests must be redone whenever the code changes; it needs no special tools and developers often do it themselves.

questions.prompt: In the CI/CD pipeline diagram, which step comes immediately before deploying changes to production?
options: Deliver the build to staging
Run the tests
Notify the test outcome
Trigger the build
Notify the build outcome
questions.explanation: The pipeline order is Commit, Trigger, Build, Notify build outcome, Run tests, Notify test outcome, Deliver build to staging, then Deploy changes to production.
